battle:diu-1509.text: February 1509, off the coast of Gujarat. A combined fleet of the Mamluks of Egypt, the Sultan of Gujarat and the ruler of Calicut, quietly backed by Venice, sets out to drive the Portuguese newcomers from the spice trade. Francisco de Almeida's ships are armed with heavy cannon, and they shatter it. It is often called the moment European naval power arrived in Asia, and it opens a century of Portuguese dominance over Asian sea trade.

battle:chaldiran.text: August 1514, in the highlands of eastern Anatolia. The Ottoman Sultan Selim the First faces Shah Ismail of Persia, whose famous horsemen have never lost a battle. But Selim has artillery, and Janissaries armed with muskets, and the Persian cavalry breaks against them. The line drawn here between the Ottoman and Persian worlds still lies close to today's border between Turkey and Iran, and it hardened the divide between Sunni and Shia.

battle:marj-dabiq.text: August 1516, near Aleppo, in Syria. Selim's guns destroy the army of the Mamluk Sultanate, and its old sultan, Qansuh al-Ghawri, dies on the field. Within months Cairo has fallen, ending a dynasty of slave-soldiers that had ruled Egypt for more than 250 years. The Ottoman Empire doubles in size, and its sultan becomes the guardian of Mecca and Medina.

battle:tenochtitlan.text: 1521. Tenochtitlan, the island capital of the Aztec Empire, stands in the middle of a great lake. Hundreds of Spaniards under Hernán Cortés, with tens of thousands of native allies, besiege it for 93 days. Smallpox has already killed huge numbers inside the city. When it falls, it is razed, and Mexico City is built on its ruins. It was the native allies, as much as Spanish steel, that decided this war.

battle:pavia.text: February 1525, in a walled hunting park near Pavia, in northern Italy. The French knights of King Francis the First charge, and Spanish arquebusiers cut them down. Francis himself is captured, and carried off to Madrid. The battle makes the Emperor Charles the Fifth master of Italy, and marks the turning point from armoured cavalry to firearms.

battle:panipat-1.text: April 1526, on the plain of Panipat, north of Delhi. Babur has come down from Kabul with a small army, but with something new to India: field guns and matchlocks. He lashes carts together as a barrier, and when his cannon fire, the war elephants of Sultan Ibrahim Lodi panic. Lodi dies on the field. The Delhi Sultanate ends here, and the Mughal Empire begins, an empire that will shape South Asia for more than 300 years.

battle:mohacs.text: August 1526, in southern Hungary. Suleiman the Magnificent's army smashes the Hungarian force in a single afternoon. The young King Louis the Second drowns in a stream as he flees, leaving no heir. Hungary is split between the Ottomans and the Habsburgs for 150 years, and the Ottoman frontier now reaches the gates of central Europe.

battle:cajamarca.text: November 1532, high in the Andes. Francisco Pizarro has just 168 men. He invites the Inca emperor, Atahualpa, to a meeting in the town square of Cajamarca, and then attacks with guns and horses. Atahualpa is captured, held for a ransom of a room full of gold, and killed anyway. An empire already weakened by civil war and smallpox loses its head, and its silver will soon fund Spain's wars in Europe.

battle:panipat-2.text: November 1556, on the same plain of Panipat. Hemu, who has taken Delhi, is winning the battle when an arrow strikes him in the eye. His army breaks. On the other side is the Mughal heir, a boy of just 13 named Akbar. Mughal rule is saved at its most fragile moment, and Akbar will reign for nearly fifty years, as the greatest of the Mughals.

battle:talikota.text: January 1565, in the Deccan of southern India. Four rival sultanates unite against the greatest power in the south, the Vijayanagara Empire. Its regent, Rama Raya, is captured and beheaded, and the magnificent city of Vijayanagara is sacked for months. Its ruins, at Hampi, are now a World Heritage Site, and the south is opened to new powers.

battle:malta-1565.text: May 1565. A great Ottoman fleet and some 35,000 men land on the island of Malta. Against them stand the Knights Hospitaller under their grand master, Jean de Valette, with Maltese soldiers, about 6,000 in all. For nearly four months they hold their forts under one of the heaviest bombardments of the age. When a small relief force finally lands, the Ottomans sail away. Malta's capital, Valletta, built afterwards, is named after the grand master.

battle:lepanto.text: October 1571, in the Gulf of Patras, off western Greece. Some 500 galleys meet, the fleets of the Holy League against the Ottoman navy, and they fight at point-blank range. In a few hours the Ottoman fleet is all but destroyed, and thousands of Christian galley slaves are set free. Among the wounded is a young soldier who loses the use of a hand: Miguel de Cervantes, the future author of Don Quixote.

battle:alcacer-quibir.text: August 1578, in northern Morocco. Portugal's young King Sebastian leads a crusade into Morocco, and his army is annihilated. Sebastian vanishes in the battle, with no heir, and two rival Moroccan sultans die too. Two years later, Philip the Second of Spain claims the Portuguese throne, and for decades, impostors appear claiming to be the lost king.

battle:armada.text: Summer, 1588. Philip the Second of Spain sends 130 ships up the English Channel, to carry an army to England. Off Gravelines, English fireships drift into the anchored fleet at night, and break its formation. Watch the Armada flee north, around Scotland, where gales wreck dozens of ships on the coast of Ireland. About 50 of the 130 never come home, and Elizabeth's Protestant England is secure.

battle:imjin-war.text: 1592. The Japanese warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi sends his samurai into Korea, on the way to attacking China. They overrun the peninsula in weeks. But Korean guerrillas, Chinese armies, and the unbeaten navy of Admiral Yi Sun-sin, with his famous turtle ships, turn them back. Yi won every one of his sea battles, and is still Korea's great national hero. Perhaps a million people died in the war.

battle:sekigahara.text: October 1600, in the fog of a mountain pass in central Japan. Two great armies, east and west, meet to decide who will rule after Hideyoshi. At the critical moment, the troops of Kobayakawa Hideaki switch sides, and the Western Army collapses within hours. Tokugawa Ieyasu becomes shogun, and Japan enters 250 years of peace and isolation.

battle:thirty-years.text: 1618. In Prague, Protestant nobles throw the emperor's officials out of a castle window. It begins a war that becomes a struggle for mastery of all Europe, fought for thirty years across the German lands. Armies, plague and famine kill perhaps a third of the people in some regions. The Peace of Westphalia that ends it is often seen as the birth of the modern idea of sovereign states.

battle:shanhai-pass.text: May 1644. Rebels have just taken Beijing, and the last Ming emperor has hanged himself. At Shanhai Pass, where the Great Wall meets the sea, General Wu Sangui makes a fateful choice. He opens the gate to the Manchus, and together they break the rebel army. The Qing move into Beijing, and will rule China until 1912.

battle:naseby.text: June 1645, in the fields of Northamptonshire. Parliament's New Model Army, disciplined and professional, under Fairfax and Oliver Cromwell, destroys King Charles the First's last main army. Four years later, the king is executed, and England becomes, for a time, a republic. Royal power in Britain will never again be what it was.

battle:mughal-maratha.text: 1681. The Mughal emperor Aurangzeb moves his whole court south, to crush the Marathas of the Deccan. He will never go home. For a quarter of a century, hill forts and raiding cavalry wear his great armies down, and after her husband's death, the queen Tarabai leads the resistance. When Aurangzeb dies in 1707, the Mughal decline begins, and the Marathas become India's leading power.

battle:vienna-1683.text: September 1683. For two months, a huge Ottoman army has besieged Vienna, and the city is close to falling. Then, from the Kahlenberg hills above, King John Sobieski of Poland leads some 18,000 horsemen down onto the Ottoman camp, his Winged Hussars at the front. It is one of the largest cavalry charges in history. This is the high tide of Ottoman power in Europe, and from here, the long retreat begins.

battle:blenheim.text: August 1704, on the Danube, in Bavaria. The Duke of Marlborough has marched his army 400 kilometres from the Low Countries, in secret, to save Vienna. With Prince Eugene of Savoy, he crushes the French and Bavarian army, and captures its commander. Louis the Fourteenth's run of victories is over, and Britain's rise as a great power begins. Winston Churchill's birthplace, Blenheim Palace, is named after it.

battle:poltava.text: July 1709, in today's Ukraine. Charles the Twelfth of Sweden has invaded Russia, but a brutal winter has worn his army down. At Poltava, Peter the Great destroys it, and Charles flees to Ottoman lands. The Swedish Empire is finished, Russia becomes the leading power of northern Europe, and Peter can build his new capital on the Baltic: St Petersburg.

battle:karnal.text: February 1739, near Delhi. Nader Shah of Persia crushes a far larger Mughal army in just three hours. In Delhi, his troops massacre tens of thousands, and he carries home the Koh-i-Noor diamond and the Peacock Throne. The Mughals' weakness is now plain for all to see, including the European trading companies.

battle:seven-years.text: 1756. A war begins that is fought on five continents, from Canada to the Philippines, and it will decide who rules overseas. Britain and Prussia face France, Austria, Russia and Spain. When the Treaty of Paris ends it, Britain holds Canada and leads in India, the world's leading colonial power. But its debts lead to new taxes, which help spark the American Revolution, and the French one too.

battle:plassey.text: Bengal, June 1757. Near the village of Palashi, about 3,000 soldiers of the East India Company, under Robert Clive, face an army of some 50,000 led by the nawab, Siraj ud-Daulah. But Clive has made a secret deal. He has promised Bengal's throne to the nawab's own commander, Mir Jafar, and when the moment comes, Mir Jafar's troops simply stand and watch. A monsoon downpour soaks the nawab's gunpowder, while the Company keeps its own dry. A trading company now holds India's richest province, and almost two centuries of British power in India have begun.

battle:quebec-1759.text: September 1759, Quebec. In the dark, General James Wolfe's soldiers climb the cliffs above the St. Lawrence by a hidden path, and at dawn they are lined up outside the city, on the Plains of Abraham. The battle takes less than an hour, and both commanders, Wolfe and the Marquis de Montcalm, die of their wounds. Within four years, French rule in Canada is over, though French-speaking Quebec remains.

battle:panipat-3.text: January 1761, Panipat, for the third time. The Maratha army, cut off from its supplies and starving, faces the forces of the Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani. A day of huge slaughter follows. Up to 100,000 soldiers and camp followers may have died, in the battle and the massacre afterwards. Maratha power in the north is broken for a decade, leaving a gap that the East India Company is quick to fill.

battle:buxar.text: October 1764, at Buxar, in Bihar. The Mughal emperor, the nawab of Awadh, and the ousted nawab of Bengal join forces against the East India Company, and lose. The next year, the emperor grants the Company the right to collect Bengal's taxes. A trading company has become a government in all but name, and Bengal's wealth will now pay for further conquest.

battle:saratoga.text: Autumn, 1777, in the forests of New York. A British army under John Burgoyne marches south from Canada, meaning to cut the rebellious colonies in two. Instead, it is surrounded in the backwoods, and nearly 6,000 men surrender. The victory convinces France to join the Americans, and a colonial revolt becomes a world war.

battle:yorktown.text: Autumn, 1781, Virginia. A French fleet closes Chesapeake Bay, while George Washington and the French general Rochambeau march their armies south. Watch the trap close around Yorktown. After three weeks of siege, Lord Cornwallis surrenders his whole army. The American War of Independence is effectively over, and two years later, Britain recognises the United States.

battle:haitian-revolution.text: 1791. On Saint-Domingue, the richest colony in the world, half a million enslaved people rise up. Under Toussaint Louverture, they defeat French, Spanish and British armies. When Napoleon sends an expedition to retake the island, yellow fever and a final defeat at Vertières in 1803 destroy it. Haiti becomes the first Black republic, and losing it helps persuade Napoleon to sell Louisiana to the United States.

battle:valmy.text: September 1792, in Champagne. An untried army of French citizens, the new soldiers of the Revolution, faces the professional armies of Prussia and Austria. Under heavy artillery fire, they hold their ground, and the invaders turn back. The next day, France declares itself a republic. The poet Goethe, who was there, is said to have called it the beginning of a new age.

battle:nile-1798.text: August 1798, Aboukir Bay, on the coast of Egypt. Napoleon's fleet lies at anchor, thinking itself safe. At dusk, Horatio Nelson attacks from an unexpected side, between the French ships and the shore. Through the night the fleet is destroyed, and the French flagship, L'Orient, blows up. Napoleon's army is left stranded in Egypt, and Britain rules the Mediterranean.

battle:seringapatam.text: May 1799, Seringapatam, the island fortress of Mysore. For decades, Tipu Sultan has resisted the East India Company, with French allies and a corps of iron-cased rockets. At midday the walls are breached, and Tipu is found dead at a gateway among his men. Britain's toughest rival in southern India is gone, and his rockets inspire Britain's own Congreve rocket.

battle:assaye.text: September 1803, in central India. Young Arthur Wellesley, the future Duke of Wellington, crosses a river by an unmarked ford, and attacks a Maratha army far larger than his own. He loses a third of his men, but wins. Years later, after all his victories, he still called this his finest work in the field. British power now spreads across central India.

battle:trafalgar.text: October 1805, off the south-west coast of Spain. Admiral Nelson drives two columns of ships straight through the line of the French and Spanish fleet. Twenty-two enemy ships are taken, without a single British ship lost. At the height of the battle, Nelson is shot on his own deck, and dies knowing he has won. Napoleon's hopes of invading Britain are over, and Britain rules the waves for a century.

battle:austerlitz.text: December 1805, in Moravia. Napoleon deliberately weakens his right wing, inviting the Russian and Austrian armies to attack it. They take the bait. Then, as the sun burns through the morning fog, he strikes their exposed centre, and breaks it. Austerlitz is still taught as a model of battlefield deception, and within a year, the thousand-year-old Holy Roman Empire is gone.

battle:borodino.text: September 1812, west of Moscow. Napoleon's Grande Armée and the Russian army under Kutuzov fight one of the bloodiest days in history. Napoleon wins the field, and marches into Moscow, only to find it burning, and empty. The retreat through the Russian winter destroys his army. Of more than 500,000 men who invaded, only a few marched back.

battle:leipzig.text: October 1813, at Leipzig, in Saxony. Almost 600,000 soldiers fight for four days, the largest battle in Europe until the First World War. Russia, Prussia, Austria and Sweden close in on Napoleon. As the French retreat, a bridge is blown up too early, trapping thousands on the wrong side of the river. Napoleon is driven out of Germany, and within months, he has given up his throne.

battle:waterloo.text: June 1815, near Brussels. Napoleon is back from exile, and all day he throws his army against the Duke of Wellington's line, along a low ridge. In the evening, the Prussians under Blücher arrive on his flank, and the Imperial Guard, for once, breaks. Twenty-three years of war are over, and so is the Napoleonic age.

battle:boyaca.text: August 1819, in Colombia. Simón Bolívar leads his army over a freezing Andean pass, in the rainy season, a crossing the Spanish thought impossible. He surprises them at a bridge at Boyacá, and three days later, Bogotá falls. It is the beginning of the end of Spain's empire in the Americas.

battle:ayacucho.text: December 1824, high in the Andes of Peru. Antonio José de Sucre's patriot army destroys the last royal army in South America, and captures the viceroy himself. Three centuries of Spanish rule on the South American mainland are over. Soon after, a new country is founded, and named after Bolívar: Bolivia.

battle:navarino.text: October 1827, Navarino Bay, in south-west Greece. The fleets of Britain, France and Russia enter the bay to enforce a truce in the Greek war of independence. A shot is fired, a battle begins, and within four hours, the Ottoman and Egyptian fleet is gone. Greek independence is secured.

battle:opium-war.text: 1839. When China's Commissioner Lin Zexu destroys the British opium being smuggled into Canton, Britain sends warships. Steam-powered gunboats sail up China's rivers, and in 1842 China signs the Treaty of Nanking. Britain gains Hong Kong, and Chinese ports are forced open to foreign trade. China remembers it as the start of a century of humiliation.

battle:mexican-american.text: 1846. After the United States annexes Texas, war with Mexico follows. American armies march all the way to Mexico City. In the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Mexico gives up California and much of today's American south-west. The United States now reaches the Pacific, but the arguments over these new lands will push it closer to civil war.

battle:taiping.text: 1850. In southern China, Hong Xiuquan, who believes he is the younger brother of Jesus, founds the Heavenly Kingdom of the Taiping, and for a decade it rules much of the south from Nanjing. Its defeat leaves whole provinces empty. The Taiping Rebellion killed somewhere between 20 and 30 million people, more than the First World War, and fatally weakened the Qing.

battle:crimean.text: 1854. Britain, France and the Ottoman Empire land in Crimea, and besiege the Russian naval port of Sevastopol for almost a year. This war gives the world the Charge of the Light Brigade, the first war reporting by telegraph, and Florence Nightingale's modern nursing. Disease kills far more than the fighting. Defeat exposes Russia's backwardness, and leads it to free its serfs.

battle:indian-rebellion.text: May 1857. At Meerut, Indian soldiers of the East India Company rise up, and march to Delhi, to proclaim the old Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar. The rebellion spreads across northern India, with leaders like the Rani of Jhansi. There are terrible massacres on both sides before Britain retakes Delhi and Lucknow. Company rule ends, the British Crown takes direct control of India, and the last Mughal emperor is exiled to Burma.

battle:solferino.text: June 1859, in Lombardy. Three monarchs lead their armies in person, and some 270,000 men fight through a long, hot day. A Swiss businessman passing by, Henry Dunant, is so shocked by the thousands of wounded left to die that he goes on to found the Red Cross. The battle is a great step towards a united Italy, and leads to the first Geneva Convention.

battle:american-civil-war.text: 1861. After Abraham Lincoln is elected president, eleven slave-holding states break away from the United States. Four years of industrial-scale war follow, with railways, rifles and ironclad ships, until the Confederacy surrenders at Appomattox. Somewhere between 620,000 and 750,000 people die. Slavery ends in the United States, and the country is bound together under a stronger federal government.

battle:gettysburg.text: July 1863, in the fields of Pennsylvania. Robert E. Lee's Confederate army has invaded the North, and for three days it fights the Union army at Gettysburg. On the last day, Pickett's Charge advances across open fields, and is cut to pieces. Lee retreats, and the South never again invades the North in force. That November, Lincoln returns here to give the Gettysburg Address.

battle:paraguayan-war.text: 1864. Paraguay's leader, Francisco Solano López, takes on three neighbours at once: Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay. The war grinds on for six years, until López is killed. By then, Paraguay has lost perhaps half its people, and most of its men. The country is left devastated for generations.

battle:koniggratz.text: July 1866, in Bohemia. The Prussian general Helmuth von Moltke brings three armies by railway to meet on the battlefield. Prussian breech-loading rifles fire several times faster than the Austrian muzzle-loaders. Austria loses the war in just seven weeks, and is pushed out of German affairs. The way is now clear for a German Empire, led by Prussia.

battle:sedan.text: September 1870, at Sedan, in the Ardennes. The Prussian and German armies encircle the French army and shell it from the hills. Emperor Napoleon the Third gives himself up, with more than 100,000 men. Months later, in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, the German Empire is proclaimed. A united Germany is born, and with it, a rivalry with France that will feed two world wars.

battle:little-bighorn.text: June 1876, beside the Little Bighorn River, in Montana. Lieutenant Colonel George Custer splits his command and attacks a huge camp of Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho, defending their land under leaders like Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse. Custer and all of the 200 or so men with him are killed. It is the greatest Native American victory of the Plains Wars, but within a few years, almost all the Plains nations have been forced onto reservations.

battle:isandlwana.text: January 1879, in Zululand. Some 20,000 Zulu warriors, armed mostly with spears and shields, overrun a British camp at the foot of the hill of Isandlwana. More than 1,300 of its defenders are killed. It is one of the worst defeats a modern army ever suffered at the hands of an indigenous force. But six months later, Britain strikes back, and the Zulu kingdom is broken up.

battle:war-of-the-pacific.text: 1879. In the Atacama Desert, a dispute over bird droppings and nitrate fertiliser becomes a war. Chile fights Peru and Bolivia, wins at sea, and even occupies Lima. Bolivia loses its whole coastline. To this day, it marks a Day of the Sea, and still keeps a navy, on Lake Titicaca.

battle:adwa.text: March 1896, in the mountains of northern Ethiopia. Emperor Menelik the Second and Empress Taytu have gathered a huge, well-armed army. The Italian columns lose their way in the mountains, and in a single day they are destroyed. Ethiopia stays independent through the whole Scramble for Africa, and Adwa becomes a symbol of African freedom.

battle:omdurman.text: September 1898, on the Nile, in Sudan. Herbert Kitchener's army has Maxim machine guns and river gunboats. In a single morning, wave after wave of Sudanese soldiers are cut down: about 10,000 killed, against fewer than 50 on the British side. A young Winston Churchill rides in one of the last British cavalry charges. It is a grim picture of the industrial firepower behind colonial conquest.

battle:spanish-american.text: 1898. After the battleship USS Maine blows up in Havana harbour, the United States goes to war with Spain. In Manila Bay, Commodore Dewey sinks the Spanish fleet in a single morning. Spain gives up Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines. Four centuries of Spanish global empire are over, and the United States emerges as a world power.

battle:boer-war.text: 1899. Britain expects a quick war over the gold fields of the Transvaal. Instead, Boer farmers on horseback fight on for almost three years. In response, Britain sweeps civilians, both Boer and Black African, into camps where tens of thousands die. The war leads to the Union of South Africa in 1910, on terms that exclude the Black majority.

battle:tsushima.text: May 1905, in the strait between Korea and Japan. After a voyage of seven months from the Baltic, the Russian fleet meets Admiral Tōgō's modern Japanese navy. Tōgō crosses the Russian line, and sinks or captures almost all of it. For the first time in the modern age, an Asian power has beaten a European great power at sea. Japan rises as an imperial power, and Russia is shaken by revolution.

battle:mexican-revolution.text: 1910. What begins as a revolt against the long rule of Porfirio Díaz becomes a decade of fighting among revolutionary factions. Peasant armies, and the photographers who follow them, turn Emiliano Zapata and Pancho Villa into legends. Around a million people die. The constitution of 1917 brings land reform and workers' rights, and shapes Mexico for the rest of the century.

battle:xinhai.text: October 1911. At Wuchang, an accidental bomb blast exposes a revolutionary plot, and a mutiny follows. Within weeks it has spread across China. In February 1912, the six-year-old emperor, Puyi, gives up the throne. More than two thousand years of imperial rule are over, and Asia's first major republic begins.

battle:balkan-wars.text: 1912. Four small Balkan kingdoms, Serbia, Greece, Bulgaria and Montenegro, join together to drive the Ottoman Empire out of Europe, and in a few months, they do. Then they fight among themselves over the spoils. Five centuries of Ottoman rule in most of the Balkans end, leaving tensions that will explode in Sarajevo, a year later.

battle:marne.text: September 1914. The German armies are sweeping towards Paris, nearly in sight of the city. Then the French and British strike into a gap that has opened in the German line. The Germans fall back to high ground and dig in. Watch the front settle. The war of movement in the west is over, and the trench line that will last until 1918 begins.

battle:gallipoli.text: April 1915. To knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war, British, French, Australian and New Zealand troops land on the cliff-lined beaches of the Gallipoli peninsula. The Ottomans hold the heights above them for eight months, until the Allies withdraw. Each side suffers about 250,000 casualties. A young officer named Mustafa Kemal rises to fame here, and the 25th of April is still remembered as Anzac Day.

battle:verdun.text: February 1916. Germany attacks Verdun, a fortress city that France feels it can never give up. For ten months, on a tiny patch of ground, the shelling never stops. Forests and villages vanish, and the land is torn apart. Some 700,000 men are killed or wounded, in the longest battle of the First World War, and Verdun becomes a lasting symbol of French resolve, and of the waste of attrition.

battle:jutland.text: May 1916, in the North Sea. About 250 warships of the British and German fleets meet in the largest naval battle of the war. Britain loses more ships and more men. Yet afterwards, the German fleet barely challenges it again, turning instead to submarines. And it is the U-boats that will bring the United States into the war.

battle:somme.text: The 1st of July, 1916. A week of bombardment has failed to cut the German wire, and British soldiers walk into machine-gun fire. It is the worst day in the history of the British Army. Over four and a half months, the Allies advance about ten kilometres, and tanks go into battle for the first time. The Somme becomes a byword for the horror of the Great War.

battle:russian-civil-war.text: 1917. After the October Revolution, civil war spreads across the whole former Russian Empire. Lenin and Trotsky's Red Army fights the White armies, with Allied expeditions joining in. Famine and disease kill far more than the fighting, between 7 and 12 million people in all. In 1922, the Soviet Union is born, the world's first communist state.

battle:turkish-independence.text: 1919. As the Allies carve up the defeated Ottoman Empire, Mustafa Kemal rallies a Turkish army in Anatolia. Greek forces are turned back at the Sakarya River, and routed in 1922. The sultanate is abolished, and Turkey becomes a republic. A huge, forced exchange of Greek and Turkish populations follows.

battle:warsaw-1920.text: August 1920. Soviet armies are at the gates of Warsaw, and Poland's newly won independence seems about to end. Then Józef Piłsudski strikes from the south, into a gap in the Soviet line. The Red Army collapses. Poland survives, and the revolution is kept from spreading west by force of arms.

battle:spanish-civil-war.text: July 1936. A military uprising splits Spain in two. Hitler and Mussolini back General Franco's Nationalists, while the Soviet Union and international volunteers help the Republic. The bombing of Guernica shocks the world. Around half a million people die, Franco rules as dictator until 1975, and the bombing tactics tested here are used across Europe a few years later.

battle:sino-japanese.text: 1937. Japan's invasion of China takes Shanghai, and then Nanjing, where its troops carry out a notorious massacre. China trades land for time, retreating to Chongqing, and for eight years ties down huge Japanese armies. Somewhere between 15 and 20 million Chinese people die. Japan's war in China leads to an American oil embargo, and from there, to Pearl Harbor.

battle:dunkirk.text: May 1940. The German breakthrough has trapped the British army and its French allies against the sea at Dunkirk. Over nine days, more than 338,000 soldiers are carried off the beaches, by destroyers, fishing boats and pleasure craft, many crossing the Channel again and again. The core of the British Army is saved, and Britain can fight on.

battle:battle-of-britain.text: Summer, 1940. To invade Britain, Hitler needs control of the skies. Day after day, RAF pilots, guided by radar, climb to meet the Luftwaffe. They hold out through the summer. Germany turns instead to bombing cities, the Blitz, and then gives up the invasion. It is Hitler's first major defeat, and Britain remains in the war.

battle:moscow-1941.text: Autumn, 1941. German scouts come so close to Moscow that they can almost see the Kremlin. Then the mud, the winter, and fresh divisions from Siberia turn the battle. A Soviet counter-attack throws the Germans back a hundred kilometres and more. Hitler's plan for a quick victory over the Soviet Union is over.

battle:pearl-harbor.text: The 7th of December, 1941, a Sunday morning in Hawaii. More than 350 Japanese planes strike the US Pacific Fleet at anchor. They sink or damage 19 ships, and 2,403 Americans are killed. But the American aircraft carriers are away at sea. The United States enters the Second World War, and within days, Germany declares war on it too.

battle:singapore-1942.text: February 1942. Japanese troops have raced down the Malay peninsula, many on bicycles. Now they cross to the island fortress of Singapore. Some 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops surrender, to a much smaller force. Churchill calls it the worst disaster in British military history, and the idea of European invincibility in Asia is shattered.

battle:midway.text: June 1942, in the central Pacific. American code-breakers know the Japanese plan. US dive-bombers catch the Japanese carriers as they refuel their planes, and within minutes, three of them are ablaze. A fourth is sunk later that day. Japan's navy never recovers its strength in carriers, and the initiative in the Pacific passes to America.

battle:stalingrad.text: August 1942. The German Sixth Army reaches Stalingrad, on the Volga. Germans and Soviets fight house by house, floor by floor, through a ruined city. In November, the Red Army strikes from north and south, and closes a ring around the Germans. In February, the survivors give in. It is the great turning point of the war in the east.

battle:el-alamein.text: October 1942, in the Egyptian desert. A thunderous night-time artillery barrage opens the battle, and Montgomery's Eighth Army fights its way through deep minefields to break Rommel's line. The German and Italian retreat ends only in Tunisia. As Churchill put it: before Alamein, we never had a victory. After Alamein, we never had a defeat.

battle:kursk.text: July 1943. Germany launches its last great offensive in the east, against a huge bulge in the Soviet line around Kursk. But warned by spies, the Soviets have dug vast belts of minefields and anti-tank guns. The German armour breaks against them, and then the Red Army counter-attacks. From here until Berlin, it is the Soviets who attack.

battle:imphal.text: Spring, 1944. Japan invades India from Burma, aiming for Imphal and Kohima. At Kohima, the two sides fight across a tennis court. Starved of supplies in the monsoon, the Japanese army is shattered, losing over half its men. The threat to India is over, and the way is open for the reconquest of Burma.

battle:normandy.text: The 6th of June, 1944. On a stormy morning, 156,000 Allied troops land on five beaches in Normandy, with 7,000 ships and 11,000 planes behind them. Follow the arrows inland. The fighting through the hedgerows is long and hard, but within three months, Paris is free. A second front has opened, and together with the Soviet advance, it dooms Nazi Germany.

battle:leyte-gulf.text: October 1944, in the waters around the Philippines. Japan commits almost its entire remaining navy to stop the American landings at Leyte. Over four days, in perhaps the largest sea battle in history, it loses 26 ships. The Imperial Japanese Navy is finished as a fighting force, Japan's oil lifeline from the south is cut, and the first organised kamikaze attacks begin.

battle:bulge.text: December 1944, in the snow-covered forests of the Ardennes. German tanks burst through the thinly held American lines, aiming to split the Allies apart. At the crossroads town of Bastogne, surrounded American troops hold out. Asked to surrender, their commander replies with a single word: nuts. The attack burns through Germany's last reserves, in the largest battle the US Army fought in that war.

battle:berlin-1945.text: April 1945. Two and a half million Soviet and Polish soldiers close in on Berlin, and storm the city street by street. On the 30th of April, in his bunker beneath the city, Hitler shoots himself. Berlin surrenders on the 2nd of May, and Germany six days later. The war in Europe is over, and the divided city will become the front line of the Cold War.

battle:hiroshima.text: August 1945. On the 6th, an American bomber drops an atomic bomb on Hiroshima. Three days later, a second destroys Nagasaki. Most of the victims die in moments, others from burns and radiation in the months that follow, somewhere between 110,000 and 210,000 people. In the same week, the Soviet Union invades Manchuria, and Japan surrenders. The Second World War is over, and the nuclear age has begun. Historians still debate the decision.

battle:chinese-civil-war.text: 1946. With Japan defeated, the old war between China's Communists and Nationalists resumes. The Communists win in Manchuria, and then, in the vast Huaihai campaign, destroy the Nationalist armies. Chiang Kai-shek flees to Taiwan. On the 1st of October 1949, Mao Zedong proclaims the People's Republic of China, and Taiwan's status remains unresolved to this day.

battle:indo-pak-1947.text: 1947. Weeks after independence and Partition, tribal fighters from Pakistan move into Kashmir, and its ruler joins India. India and Pakistan go to war. A United Nations ceasefire leaves the region divided, along a line that still splits it today. Kashmir has been a source of conflict between the two neighbours ever since.

battle:arab-israeli-1948.text: May 1948. As British rule ends, Israel declares its independence, and the armies of neighbouring Arab states invade. Israel holds on, and expands. Some 700,000 Palestinians flee or are driven from their homes. Israel's borders are set by ceasefire lines, not peace treaties, and the refugee question remains at the heart of the conflict.

battle:korean-war.text: June 1950. North Korea's army sweeps south, almost to the tip of the peninsula at Pusan. Then General MacArthur lands behind it at Incheon, and drives north to the Chinese border. China enters the war, and pushes the UN forces back again. After three years, it ends in an armistice, never a peace treaty. Korea is still divided, along the most heavily armed border in the world.

battle:algerian-war.text: 1954. In Algeria, the National Liberation Front begins a war for independence from France. It is a brutal war of guerrillas, bombs and torture. It topples France's Fourth Republic, brings Charles de Gaulle back to power, and ends in 1962 with Algeria's independence. Almost a million French settlers leave, after 132 years of French rule.

battle:dien-bien-phu.text: March 1954. France drops troops into a remote valley in north-west Vietnam, hoping to lure the Viet Minh into a set-piece battle. But General Giáp's men haul artillery by hand up the surrounding hills, and after 56 days, they overrun the base. French Indochina is finished, and Vietnam is divided at Geneva.

battle:vietnam-war.text: 1955. A war for the future of Vietnam begins, between the communist North and the American-backed South. At its peak, more than 500,000 US troops are fighting there. The Tet Offensive of 1968 turns opinion at home. The Americans leave in 1973, and two years later, North Vietnamese tanks roll into Saigon. Somewhere between 2 and 3 million people die, and Vietnam is united under communist rule.

battle:suez.text: 1956. Egypt's leader, Gamal Abdel Nasser, takes over the Suez Canal. Britain, France and Israel secretly plot an invasion, and on the ground, it succeeds. But the United States and the Soviet Union force them to withdraw. Britain's prime minister, Anthony Eden, resigns, Nasser becomes the hero of the Arab world, and it is plain that Britain is no longer a superpower.

battle:bay-of-pigs.text: April 1961. About 1,400 Cuban exiles, trained and backed by the CIA, land at the Bay of Pigs to overthrow Fidel Castro. The air support they expect never comes, and within three days, Castro's forces have them trapped on the beach. It is a humiliation for President Kennedy, and it pushes Cuba closer to Moscow, towards the missile crisis of 1962.

battle:sino-indian.text: October 1962, high in the Himalayas. China strikes at both ends of a disputed border, at Aksai Chin in the west, and in what is now Arunachal Pradesh in the east. After a month, China declares a ceasefire, and pulls back in the east. The border is still disputed, and the two armies have clashed there as recently as 2020.

battle:six-day-war.text: June 1967. A surprise Israeli air strike destroys Egypt's air force on the ground. In less than a week, Israel takes Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights. Sinai is returned to Egypt after the peace of 1979, but the status of the West Bank, Gaza and the Golan remains central to the conflict today.

battle:bangladesh-1971.text: March 1971. A brutal crackdown in East Pakistan sends 10 million refugees across the border into India. Hundreds of thousands, by some counts millions, die in the killing. In December, India enters the war, and within thirteen days, Pakistan's forces surrender, the largest surrender since the Second World War. A new country is born: Bangladesh.

battle:yom-kippur.text: October 1973. On Yom Kippur, Judaism's holiest day, Egypt and Syria attack, and Egyptian troops cross the Suez Canal. Israel recovers, and pushes back across the canal. Arab oil producers then cut supplies to the West, and the oil embargo shakes the world economy. In time, the war leads to the Camp David Accords, and peace between Egypt and Israel.

battle:soviet-afghan.text: December 1979. Soviet troops roll into Afghanistan to prop up a communist government. They are bogged down for ten years, fighting mujahideen guerrillas armed by the United States, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. Somewhere between one and two million people die, and millions become refugees. The war helps bring on the collapse of the Soviet Union, and paves the way for the Taliban.

battle:iran-iraq.text: September 1980. Saddam Hussein invades the newly revolutionary Iran, expecting quick gains. Instead, the war drags on for eight years, with trenches and poison gas. Half a million or more people die, and when it ends, the border is about where it started. Iraq is left deep in debt, and two years later, it invades Kuwait.

battle:falklands.text: April 1982. Argentina's military government seizes the Falkland Islands, which it calls the Malvinas. Britain sends a fleet 13,000 kilometres south. After a war of 74 days, the islands are retaken. Argentina's military government falls, and democracy returns in 1983. Sovereignty is still disputed.

battle:gulf-war.text: August 1990. Iraq takes over Kuwait. A huge coalition led by the United States gathers, and in January it launches weeks of air attacks. The ground war, when it comes, lasts just 100 hours, and Kuwait is freed. Precision weapons and live cable news change how war is seen, but Saddam Hussein stays in power.

battle:yugoslav-wars.text: 1991. As Yugoslavia breaks apart, wars of ethnic cleansing tear the region apart. Sarajevo is besieged for almost four years, and at Srebrenica, about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys are killed. Some 130,000 people die across the decade. International courts later convict leaders of war crimes, and of genocide at Srebrenica. Seven countries now stand where one once was.

battle:second-congo.text: 1998. Rooted in the aftermath of the Rwandan genocide, and in a struggle for minerals, a war draws in the armies of nine countries in and around the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It becomes the deadliest war since 1945, with estimates of up to five million dead, most of them from hunger and disease. Fighting in the east of the country continues even now.

battle:kargil.text: May 1999, high in the mountains of Ladakh. Pakistani soldiers and militants secretly occupy ridges overlooking India's key road to Ladakh. India takes them back, at heavy cost, climbing through snow and thin air, and international pressure brings a Pakistani withdrawal. It is a rare direct war between two nuclear-armed states.

battle:afghanistan-2001.text: October 2001. After the attacks of the 11th of September, the United States topples the Taliban in Afghanistan within weeks. Then comes a twenty-year insurgency. In 2021, as American forces leave, the Afghan government collapses within days, and the Taliban return to power. By one major estimate, about 176,000 or more people died directly in the fighting.

battle:iraq-2003.text: March 2003. A coalition led by the United States and Britain invades Iraq, justified by weapons of mass destruction that are never found. Baghdad falls within weeks. A sectarian civil war follows, which later gives rise to the so-called Islamic State. Hundreds of thousands of Iraqis die, and the Middle East is reshaped.

battle:syrian-civil-war.text: 2011. In Syria, Arab Spring protests are met with brutal force, and become a many-sided war that draws in Russia, Iran, Turkey and the United States, and gives rise to ISIS. More than half the population is forced from their homes. In December 2024, a rapid rebel offensive takes Damascus, ending 53 years of rule by the Assad family. This account is as of early 2026.

battle:russia-ukraine.text: February 2022. Building on its seizure of Crimea in 2014, Russia launches a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Ukraine holds Kyiv, and wins back ground that year, and the war then becomes a grinding contest of trenches and drones. Hundreds of thousands of soldiers are thought to have been killed or wounded, and millions forced from their homes. Finland and Sweden have joined NATO. This account is as of early 2026.

battle:sudan-2023.text: April 2023. In Sudan, two military rulers who had seized power together turn on each other in the capital, Khartoum. The fighting spreads to Darfur, with mass atrocities reported, and famine declared. According to the United Nations, more than 10 million people have been forced from their homes. This account is as of early 2026.

battle:gaza-2023.text: October 2023. On the 7th, Hamas-led fighters attack southern Israel, killing about 1,200 people and taking some 250 hostages. Israel's air and ground offensive devastates Gaza, where local health officials count more than 60,000 dead. The war draws in Lebanon, Iran and Yemen's Houthis, and is the subject of cases at international courts. A fragile ceasefire began in October 2025. This account is as of early 2026.
